title: Lesson 4: Intervals as Shapes
intro: An interval is the distance between two notes (see Intervals (#/arts/music-theory/intervals)). On the guitar every interval is a fixed finger shape that works anywhere on the neck. Once you know the shapes from a root on strings 6 and 5, you can build any chord or scale from its intervals.

items: Play every interval from a root on string 6.
Use the same shapes from string 5.
Adjust shapes that cross from the G string to the B string.
Lesson 3 (note names on strings 6 and 5) and the idea of a root (#/arts/music-theory/chords/roots).

Step 1. Play A on string 6 fret 5. Count frets up the same string: 1 fret = minor second (B♭), 2 = major second (B), 3 = minor third (C), 4 = major third (C♯), 5 = perfect fourth (D), 7 = perfect fifth (E), 12 = octave (A).
Step 2. Play each one after the root and listen: the minor third sounds dark, the major third bright, the fifth open and strong.
Step 1. Keep the root A on string 6 fret 5 with your first finger. The same fret on string 5 (D) is a perfect fourth.
Step 2. One fret back on string 5 (fret 4, C♯) is a major third; two frets back (fret 3, C) is a minor third.
Step 3. Two frets up on string 5 (fret 7, E) is the perfect fifth. Root plus fifth is the power chord shape.
Step 4. On string 4: one fret back (fret 4, F♯) is a major sixth; the same fret (fret 5, G) a minor seventh; one fret up (fret 6, G♯) a major seventh; two frets up (fret 7, A) the octave.
Step 5. Step through the example below; each step is root, interval, then both together.

blocks.alt: A section of the neck from fret 3 to 9 with the root A on string 6 fret 5 in red and blue dots labelled with interval names: M2, m3 and M3 along string 6; m3, M3, P4, tritone, P5 and m6 on string 5; M6, m7, M7 and the octave on string 4.
blocks.caption: Every interval above a root on string 6, as fixed positions. The same picture works from a root on string 5 (shift it one string over).

widget.title: Interval shapes from A on string 6, fret 5

examples.label: Minor 7th (G): two strings up, same fret

items: Step 1. Root A on string 4 fret 7. Its fifth on string 3 is two frets up: fret 9 (E). Same shape as before, because the D and G strings are a fourth apart.
Step 2. Now root G on string 3 fret 0 (open). Its fifth on string 2 should be two frets up, but string 2 is only a major third above string 3, so add one fret: fret 3 (D).
Step 3. Rule: any shape that reaches onto the B string (or the high e from below the B) moves up one fret on those strings.

blocks.text: A major chord is root + major third + fifth. Put the root on string 6, the fifth on string 5 two frets up, the octave on string 4 two frets up, and the major third on string 3 one fret up from the root's fret: that is the E-shape barre chord (Lesson 5). Lower that third one fret and it becomes minor. Lower the octave on string 4 by two frets and it becomes a dominant seventh.

items: 4 min: from roots G, A, C and D on string 6, play the minor 3rd, major 3rd, 5th and octave, saying the interval names.
4 min: the same from roots C, D and E on string 5.
2 min: root on string 3, fifth on string 2 (remember the extra fret).

blocks.title: Find the third
blocks.text: Your root is C on string 5 fret 3. Where is the major third on string 4, and the minor third?
solution: String 4 is a fourth above string 5. A major third is one semitone less than a fourth: one fret back, string 4 fret 2 (E). Minor third: two frets back, fret 1 (E♭).

blocks.title: Across G–B
blocks.text: Root G on string 3 (open). Where is its perfect fifth on string 2?
solution: Normally two frets up; crossing G–B adds one: string 2 fret 3 (D).

blocks.text: Sources: Goodrick, M. (1987). The Advancing Guitarist. Hal Leonard; Tagliarino, B. (2006). Guitar Fretboard Workbook. Hal Leonard; Leavitt, W. G. (1966–1971). A Modern Method for Guitar, vols. 1–3. Berklee Press.
